regions.name: Western Europe (France)
regions.why: Heat waves and droughts have hit Western Europe repeatedly since 2003.

T2M.label: Air temperature
T2M.simple: How warm the air is 2 metres above the ground — what a thermometer in the shade shows.

PRECTOTCORR.label: Precipitation
PRECTOTCORR.simple: How much rain and snow falls, in millimetres of water per day (1 mm on one square metre is one litre). MERRA-2 corrects its model rain with rain gauges and satellite observations.

GWETROOT.label: Root-zone soil wetness
GWETROOT.simple: How wet the soil is where plant roots drink (roughly the top metre): 0 % is bone dry, 100 % is completely soaked.

EVLAND.label: Evaporation from land
EVLAND.simple: Water rising from the land into the air — from wet soil, lakes and plant leaves (transpiration) — in millimetres per day.

ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.label: Sunlight at the surface
ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.simple: How much solar energy reaches the ground through clouds and haze, per square metre and per day.

CLOUD_AMT.label: Cloud cover
CLOUD_AMT.simple: The percentage of the sky covered by clouds.

keywords.definition: (Also called hot wave, warm wave.) A period of abnormally and uncomfortably hot and usually humid weather. To be a heat wave such a period should last at least one day, but conventionally it lasts from several days to several weeks. In 1900, A. T. Burrows more rigidly defined a 'hot wave' as a spell of three or more days on each of which the maximum shade temperature reaches or exceeds 90°F. More realistically, the comfort criteria for any one region are dependent upon the normal conditions of that region. In the eastern United States, heat waves generally build up with southerly winds on the western flank of an anticyclone centered over the southeastern states, the air being warmed by passage over a land surface heated by the sun.

story.text: Air temperature — Western Europe (France): +0.42 °C per decade (95 % range +0.308 to +0.525). Significant rising trend: both tests agree at the 95 % level. Mann-Kendall p = 3.7e-08, t-test p = 2.1e-05. Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (+0.401 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, 79 % of months came out higher than Eva's norm expected from their neighbours (50 % if nothing had changed): the dynamic has left the norm she learned in 1981–2010.

Root-zone soil wetness: around 1988 the trend turned upward in 31 of 268 grid cells at once (chance gathers as many cells, anywhere, of any type, 0.01 of the time or less). Not on one of MERRA-2's stream joins; still a reanalysis, to be checked against independent data.

Root-zone soil wetness and Evaporation from land leave their norm in the same months, the same way: 49 times, where chance at the same moment of the record would give 28 (p = 1e-05; z = 7.7 against the same reading with one of them moved 1 to 5 years, beyond the shared trend and the persistence of each). Model note: MERRA-2's land model computes evaporation from the water it holds in the soil, and is driven by observation-corrected precipitation: this link is partly the model's own land physics.

story.text: Sunlight at the surface — Western Europe (France): +0.26 MJ/m²/day per decade (95 % range +0.138 to +0.358). Significant rising trend: both tests agree at the 95 % level. Mann-Kendall p = 0.00012, t-test p = 3.4e-06. Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1984 to 2025 (+0.24 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings.
Inside Western Europe (France), precipitation rises in 66 grid cells and falls in 206: reading the field from cell to cell, Eva found 6 out-of-norm transitions where the trend reverses.
Inside Western Europe (France), evaporation from land rises in 113 grid cells and falls in 155: reading the field from cell to cell, Eva found 7 out-of-norm transitions where the trend reverses.
